scope: inventory.json groups.persistence; read-only persistence, adapters, migrations and their tests

findings.title: Proof issuance and role changes acquire target identity/membership locks in opposite orders
findings.evidence: issue_proof locks the requesting users row FOR UPDATE and its memberships row FOR SHARE in one join. A role change updates the affected membership with set_role before retire_sessions locks the affected users row FOR UPDATE. Organization serialization protects membership mutations against one another, but issue_proof does not participate in that serialization. With owner A changing member B: the role-change transaction can hold B membership while B proof issuance holds B user and waits for B membership; role-change then waits for B user. The lock cycle is membership -> user -> membership. storage::Failure maps PostgreSQL 40P01 to an unavailable result; there is no transaction retry in the application flow.
findings.consequence: Ordinary concurrent proof requests and role changes can deadlock and abort an otherwise valid privileged operation (or proof request). This also makes the existing global user/session/membership lock discipline unsafe to extend across organizations.
findings.authority: CONTRIBUTING.md:5 assigns authoritative locks to infrastructure; ADR 001:7 and 15 require atomic authority changes and credential retirement. Existing owner_race test covers competing changes under one organization lock, not proof-versus-change lock order.
findings.remedy: Define one explicit acquisition order for organization, all involved users, sessions and memberships; acquire affected identity locks before changing membership, with deterministic ordering for multiple users and without later SHARE-to-UPDATE upgrades. Preserve login serialization and final authority checks. A simpler shared organization gate for proof issuance is an option only after accounting for shared users across organizations; do not assume a per-tenant gate solves all cross-tenant user-lock cycles.
findings.verification: Add a real-PostgreSQL barrier-controlled regression with owner A and member B. Hold the target membership at the pre-retirement boundary, start B proof issuance, observe the wait with pg_blocking_pids, and allow retirement. Require both valid operations to finish without 40P01/Unavailable, or an explicit authority rejection if the role-change retires B session first. Also exercise two organizations sharing actors and concurrent login. No arbitrary sleeps; run with runtime-role connections.
findings.verification_status: Source-traced lock cycle; not dynamically reproduced in this review. Full-suite/database fixture ownership remains with parent.

findings.title: Session enumeration silently hides live credentials after the first hundred
findings.evidence: The only session list query orders by created_at DESC and applies LIMIT 100. The port and HTTP endpoint return an unqualified Vec of IDs with no cursor or has-more indicator. Login inserts a new session on every valid link and enforces no active-session count bound. Existing sessions can remain idle-live by activity; the login mailbox rate limit bounds issuance rate, not total live sessions. Consequently a legitimate older live session can never appear in a repeated list call while newer live sessions remain.
findings.consequence: Account owners cannot enumerate all active credentials or discover/select an older suspicious session for targeted revocation. The available revoke-all action is a disruptive workaround, not a complete implementation of live-session listing.
findings.authority: AUTH-02 explicitly includes session listing and revocation; Authentication::sessions documents listing the authenticated account live sessions without disclosing truncation. ADR 001:15 promises live-session lists.
findings.remedy: Add bounded keyset pagination with a stable unique ordering and expose the continuation contract through application, HTTP and generated SDK. Alternatively introduce an explicitly approved active-session cap at admission, but do not silently substitute one for the other. Keep live/owner predicates on every page.
findings.verification: Seed at least 101 simultaneously live sessions for one user plus another user, with deterministic timestamps and a tie case. Traverse the public endpoint to completion, prove every owned live ID occurs exactly once, exclude expired/revoked/foreign rows, and revoke an ID formerly hidden beyond the first page.
findings.verification_status: Exact query and public caller signature inspected; no runtime fixture seeded.

findings.title: Security-critical SQL is compressed into opaque query/bind/error chains instead of reviewable operations
findings.evidence: The auth, memberships and projects adapters contain respectively 5, 6 and 4 physical lines longer than 300 characters; longest lines are 445, 523 and 517 characters. Those lines combine SQL predicates, join and locking clauses, positional parameter binding, execution and error conversion. Near-identical live-user/session predicates are repeated in actor validation, current-role lookup, invitation acceptance and proof issuance, with different locks. Only four project/organization write statements have SQLx offline metadata; the most complex identity queries are runtime-checked. Small file line counts therefore conceal the actual query and authority complexity.
findings.consequence: Security changes require comparing dense positional SQL chains across multiple files. It is unusually easy to miss a different expiry predicate, lock mode/order, tenant binding or execution boundary. This directly obstructs reviewing and repairing PERSIST-1; passing rustfmt/Clippy and sub-200-line file sizes do not establish maintainable operations.
findings.authority: CONTRIBUTING.md:5 and ADR 001:7 assign authoritative lock/publication safeguards to these adapters. Engineering contract requires visible side effects, cohesive boundaries and readable invariant enforcement, not line-count compression.
findings.remedy: Make each SQL statement a multiline raw string or a narrowly named query source; put bind, fetch and mapping steps on separate lines, and use private typed row projections for meaningful results. Group login/budgets and session lifecycle as cohesive private modules if needed. Establish a small explicit locked-identity primitive only where the semantics truly match; retain purpose-specific lock strengths and transaction boundaries instead of creating a generic query builder or one configurable authorization mega-query. Extend checked query metadata where feasible and regenerate it from source, never hand-edit it.
findings.verification: Preserve the real database auth/session/proof/owner-race/transaction suites, add the lock-order regression, run query preparation and offline compilation, and review the resulting operations side by side to ensure all predicates/bind orders/lock modes remain equivalent. Structural acceptance is readable security checks with no hidden modes, not simply moving the same long strings into constants.
findings.verification_status: Programmatic physical-line measurements and complete source inspection; no production edits or test runs.

additional_risks_not_promoted_to_finding.detail: Time predicates are evaluated in locking SELECT/UPDATE statements and there are later waits before commit. A barrier-controlled near-expiry test should distinguish valid admission-time linearization from a token/session already expired when its initial lock is finally obtained. This review did not dynamically establish PostgreSQL recheck behavior for the exact query plans, so it does not claim a proven expiry bypass.

Cleanup removes expired magic links, proofs and budgets but never sessions or revocation handles. Proof admission counts by user_id/expiry without a supporting index. These are capacity/retention concerns requiring an explicit retention contract and representative EXPLAIN/load evidence; no performance numbers or mandatory retention duration are invented here.

positive_assessments: Every assigned path was inspected, including clean files and four generated SQLx metadata files checked against actual source queries and migrations.
Application owns role/last-owner decisions; infrastructure owns scoped transactions and locked final authority. Do not move these safeguards out of the transaction in pursuit of a thinner adapter.
SQLx and official River own migration, queue and retry machinery; enqueue uses the same transaction as business/audit writes. No replacement infrastructure is justified.

Tenant tables use FORCE RLS and transaction-local context; discovery adds SELECT-only self policies, and runtime bootstrap rejects superuser/BYPASSRLS/table-owner connections. Credentials/proofs are intentionally global identity records, not ordinary tenant data.
Session revocation lineage resolves immutable identity before the update; the existing lock-observed rotation/logout regression meaningfully exercises that race.
Proof consumption binds user/session/action/target/organization and shares the mutation transaction; role changes serialize login through the user row and retire affected credentials.
Mail transport reuses Lettre with required verified STARTTLS; SMTP retry/token replacement ambiguity is explicitly documented rather than advertised as exactly once.

Redis is bounded by command deadlines, namespaced by environment/tenant, and never authoritative for membership/session state. Eventual cache consistency is an explicit ADR tradeoff, not a new defect.

Existing adapter tests cover real PostgreSQL/RLS, proof binding, single-winner consumption, last-owner races, SMTP certificate rejection, Redis failures, and real River crash/rescue. This review did not rerun them or infer a current passing baseline.
